paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence, trying to look dignified, and waited for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he had wanted to meet him for a long time. The boys had told him a great deal about Alyosha. Until now he had always put on a show of scornful indifference whenever Alyosha was mentioned, and he had even “criticized” what he heard. But secretly he longed to get to know him. Everything he was told about Alyosha was appealing and likable. So this moment mattered. To begin with, he had to show himself at his best and show his independence. “Or he’ll think I’m thirteen and take me for a boy, like the rest of them. And what are these boys to him? I’ll ask him once I know him better. It’s a pity I’m so short, though. Tuzikov is younger than I am, yet he’s half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I’m not good-looking. I know I’m hideous, but I’ve a clever face. I mustn’t talk too freely. If I throw myself into his arms all at once, he may think—Tfoo! How horrible if he should think—!”

These were the thoughts that stirred Kolya up while he did his utmost to look as independent as he could. What distressed him most was being so short. He did not mind his “hideous” face so much as his height. In a corner at home the year before, he had made a pencil mark on the wall to show how tall he was, and every two months since then he had anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he had gained. But alas, he grew very slowly, and this sometimes brought him almost to despair. His face was in fact by no means “hideous.” On the contrary, it was rather attractive, with fair, pale, freckled skin. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often glowed with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones and small, very red lips that were not very thick. His nose was small and unmistakably turned up. “I’ve a regular pug nose, a regular pug nose,” Kolya would mutter to himself when he looked in the mirror, and he always walked away from it indignant. “But perhaps I haven’t got a clever face?” he sometimes thought, doubting even that. But you must not suppose that his mind was taken up with his face and his height. On the contrary, however bitter the moments in front of the mirror were, he quickly forgot them, and forgot them for a long time, “abandoning himself entirely to ideas and to real life,” as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried over to Kolya. Before he reached him, Kolya could see that he looked delighted. “Can he really be so glad to see me?” Kolya wondered, feeling pleased. A word in passing: Alyosha’s appearance had changed completely since we last saw him. He had given up his cassock and now wore a well-cut coat and a soft round hat, and his hair was cropped short. All this suited him very well, and he looked quite handsome. His charming face always had a good-humored expression, but there was a gentleness and calm in his good humor. To Kolya’s surprise, Alyosha came out to him just as he was, without an overcoat. He had obviously come in a hurry. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
“Here you are at last! We’ve been so eager to see you!”

“There were reasons, which you’ll hear in a moment. Anyway, I’m glad to meet you. I’ve been hoping for a chance for a long time, and I’ve heard a great deal about you,” Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
“We would have met anyway. I’ve heard a lot about you, too, but you’ve been a long time coming here.”
“Tell me, how are things going?”
“Ilusha is very ill. He’s certainly dying.”
“How awful! You have to admit that medicine is a fraud, Karamazov,” cried Kolya hotly.

“Ilusha has talked about you often, very often, even in his sleep, when he’s delirious, you know. You can tell you used to be very, very dear to him ... before the incident ... with the knife.... And there’s another reason.... Tell me, is that your dog?”
“Yes, Perezvon.”
“Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. “Is she gone for good?”

“I know you’d all like it to be Zhutchka. I’ve heard the whole story.” Kolya smiled mysteriously. “Listen, Karamazov, I’ll tell it to you myself. That’s what I came for. That’s why I asked you to come out here: to explain the whole episode before we go in,” he began with animation. “You see, Karamazov, Ilusha joined the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is—a crowd of small boys. They started teasing him right away. I’m two classes higher up, so of course I only watched them from a distance. I saw that the boy was small and weak, but he wouldn’t give in to them. He fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they teased him all the more. The worst of it was that he was dressed horribly then. His breeches were too small, and his boots had holes in them. They hounded him about it and jeered at him. That I can’t stand. I stood up for him at once and gave it to them hot. I beat them up, but they adore me, you know, Karamazov?” Kolya boasted impulsively. “Anyway, I’m always fond of children. I’ve got two chicks to look after at home right now—that’s what held me up today. So they stopped beating Ilusha, and I took him under my wing. I saw he was proud. I tell you, the boy was proud. But in the end he became slavishly devoted to me. He did whatever I asked, obeyed me as if I were God, tried to copy me. Between classes he’d run straight to me, and I’d walk around with him. On Sundays, too. People always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that, but that’s a prejudice. If it suits me, that’s enough. I’m teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn’t I develop him if I like him? Look at you, Karamazov, taking up with all these nestlings. I can see you want to influence the younger generation—to develop them, to be useful to them. And I assure you, I’d heard about this trait of yours, and it attracted me more than anything else. But let’s get to the point. I noticed a sort of softness and sentimentality coming over the boy. And you know, I positively hate this sheepish sentimentality. I’ve hated it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him, too. He was proud, but he was slavishly devoted to me, and yet all at once his eyes would flash and he’d refuse to agree with me. He’d argue and fly into a rage. Sometimes I’d put forward certain ideas, and I could see it wasn’t so much that he disagreed with them. He was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool toward his affection. And so, to train him properly, the tenderer he was, the colder I became. I did it on purpose. That was my idea. My aim was to form his character, to knock him into shape, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you understand me at a word. Then one day I noticed that for three days running he was downcast and dejected. It wasn’t because of my coldness. It was something else, something more important. I wondered what the tragedy was. I pumped him and found out that he’d somehow got to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father—this was before his death, of course. Smerdyakov had taught the little fool a silly trick—that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs that snap up anything without chewing, and then to watch what would happen. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there’s been such a fuss about. The people of the house it belonged to never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can’t stand it.) So it rushed at the bread, swallowed it, and began to squeal. It spun round and round, then ran off, squealing, until it was out of sight. That was Ilusha’s own account. He confessed it to me and cried bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, ‘He ran away squealing.’ The sight haunted him. He was tormented by remorse, I could see that. I took it seriously. I decided to teach him a lesson for other things as well. So I have to admit I wasn’t quite straightforward, and I pretended to be more indignant than I perhaps was. ‘You’ve done a nasty thing,’ I said. ‘You’re a scoundrel. Of course I won’t tell on you, but I’m going to have nothing to do with you for a while. I’ll think it over and let you know through Smurov’—that’s the boy who just came with me, he’s always ready to do anything for me—‘whether I’ll have anything to do with you in the future or give you up for good as a scoundrel.’ He was tremendously upset. I have to own I felt I’d gone too far as I spoke, but there was no help for it. I did what I thought best at the time. A day or two later I sent Smurov to tell him I would not speak to him again. That’s what we call it when two schoolfellows break off all dealings with each other. Secretly I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days and then, if I saw signs of repentance, to hold out my hand to him again. That was my intention. But what do you think happened? He heard Smurov’s message, and his eyes flashed. ‘Tell Krassotkin from me,’ he cried, ‘that I’ll throw bread with pins to all the dogs—all—all of them!’ ‘So he’s going in for a bit of temper,’ I thought. ‘We’ll have to smoke it out of him.’ And I began to treat him with contempt. Whenever I met him I turned away or smiled sarcastically. And just then that affair with his father happened. You remember? You have to realize he was already fearfully worked up by what had gone before. The boys, seeing I’d given him up, set on him and taunted him, shouting, ‘Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!’ Soon he was having regular skirmishes with them, which I’m very sorry about. They seem to have given him one very bad beating. One day he flew at them all as they came out of school. I stood a few yards off, looking on. And I swear, I don’t remember laughing. It was quite the other way. I felt awfully sorry for him, and in another minute I’d have run over to take his side. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don’t know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and stabbed at my thigh, here in my right leg. I didn’t move. I don’t mind owning I can be plucky sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him with contempt, as if to say, ‘This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again, if you like, I’m at your service.’ But he didn’t stab me again. He broke down. He was frightened at what he’d done. He threw away the knife, burst out crying, and ran off. I didn’t sneak on him, of course, and I made them all keep quiet so it wouldn’t reach the masters. I didn’t even tell my mother till it had healed. And the wound was a mere scratch. And then I heard that the same day he’d been throwing stones and had bitten your finger—but you understand now what a state he was in! Well, it can’t be helped. It was stupid of me not to come and forgive him—that is, to make it up with him—when he fell ill. I’m sorry for it now. But I had a special reason. So now I’ve told you everything ... but I’m afraid it was stupid of me.”

“Oh, what a pity,” exclaimed Alyosha with feeling, “that I didn’t know earlier how things stood between you and him! I’d have come to you long ago to beg you to go to him with me. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I didn’t know how much you meant to him! And you really haven’t managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been searching all over town for it. Would you believe it, since he’s been ill I’ve heard him three times say, in tears, ‘It’s because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I’m ill now. God is punishing me for it.’ He can’t get that idea out of his head. And if the dog were found and proved to be alive, you could almost imagine the joy would cure him. We’ve all rested our hopes on you.”
“Tell me, what made you hope I’d be the one to find him?” Kolya asked, with great curiosity. “Why did you count on me and not on someone else?”

“There was a rumor that you were looking for the dog and would bring it once you’d found it. Smurov said something like that. We’ve all been trying to persuade Ilusha that the dog is alive and has been seen. The boys brought him a live hare. He just looked at it with a faint smile and asked them to let it go in the fields. And so we did. His father has just this moment come back, bringing him a mastiff pup, hoping to comfort him with it. But I think that only makes things worse.”
“Tell me, Karamazov, what kind of man is the father? I know him, but what do you make of him—a mountebank, a buffoon?”

“Oh, no. Some people have deep feelings and have somehow been crushed. In them, buffoonery is a bitter irony aimed at the people they’re afraid to tell the truth, because for years those people have humiliated and cowed them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that kind of buffoonery can be tragic in the extreme. His whole life now is centered on Ilusha. If Ilusha dies, he will either go mad with grief or kill himself. I’m almost sure of it when I look at him now.”
“I understand you, Karamazov. I see you understand human nature,” Kolya added warmly.
“And as soon as I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing Zhutchka.”

“Wait a bit, Karamazov, maybe we’ll find her yet. But this is Perezvon. I’ll let him go in now, and perhaps he’ll amuse Ilusha more than the mastiff pup. Wait a bit, Karamazov, you’ll see in a minute. But I say, I’m keeping you here!” Kolya cried suddenly. “You’ve no overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we’re all egoists, Karamazov!”
“Don’t worry. It is cold, but I hardly ever catch cold. Let’s go in, though. And by the way, what’s your name? I know they call you Kolya, but what else?”
“Nikolay—Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they put it in official papers, ‘Krassotkin son.’” Kolya laughed for some reason, then added suddenly, “Of course I hate the name Nikolay.”
“Why is that?”
“It’s so trivial, so ordinary.”
“You’re thirteen?” asked Alyosha.

“No, fourteen—that is, I’ll be fourteen very soon, in two weeks. I’ll confess one weakness of mine, Karamazov, just to you, since it’s our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age. More than that ... and in fact ... there’s a libelous story going around about me, that last week I played robbers with the preparatory boys. It’s a fact that I did play with them, but it’s a perfect libel to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reasons to think you’ve heard the story. But I wasn’t playing for my own amusement. It was for the children’s sake, because they couldn’t think of anything to do by themselves. But they always have some silly tale. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you.”
“But what if you had been playing for your own amusement? What’s the harm?”
“Come now, for my own amusement! You don’t play horses, do you?”

“But you have to look at it this way,” said Alyosha, smiling. “Grown-up people go to the theater, and there the adventures of all sorts of heroes are acted out—sometimes there are robbers and battles, too. Isn’t that just the same thing, in a different form, of course? And young people’s games of soldiers or robbers at playtime are also art in its first stage. You know, they spring from the growing artistic instincts of the young. And sometimes these games are much better than performances in the theater. The only difference is that people go there to look at the actors, while in these games the young people are the actors themselves. But that’s only natural.”

“You think so? Is that your idea?” Kolya looked at him intently. “Oh, you know, that’s rather an interesting view. When I get home, I’ll think it over. I’ll admit I thought I might learn something from you. I’ve come to learn from you, Karamazov,” Kolya concluded, in a voice full of spontaneous feeling.
“And I from you,” said Alyosha, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was very pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly as an equal and talked to him just as if he were “quite grown up.”
“I’ll show you something in a moment, Karamazov. It’s a theatrical performance, too,” he said, laughing nervously. “That’s why I’ve come.”
“Let’s go first to the people of the house, on the left. All the boys leave their coats in there, because the room is small and hot.”

“Oh, I’m only coming in for a minute. I’ll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the passage and be dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how he’s dead. I’ll go in first and scout around, then I’ll whistle to him when I think the time is right, and you’ll see, he’ll dash in like mad. Only Smurov mustn’t forget to open the door at the right moment. I’ll arrange it all, and you’ll see something.”
